African-American History. The lived experience of Black Americans from enslavement through the present, marked by systematic oppression, resilience, and repeated struggles for freedom and equality. This history is central to understanding American identity, constitutional evolution, and the meaning of democracy itself.

It began with forced arrival. Africans arrived in Virginia in sixteen nineteen and were gradually enslaved in larger numbers as colonial economies demanded labor. By seventeen hundred, slavery had become a racial institution. By eighteen sixty, there were over four million enslaved African Americans—the largest forced population movement in human history.

The Civil War and the Thirteenth Amendment ended slavery, but Reconstruction-era progress was reversed by Jim Crow Laws that entrenched segregation and disenfranchisement. It wasn't until the nineteen fifties and sixties that the Civil Rights Movement challenged segregation through nonviolent protest, legislation, and legal victories like Brown v. Board of Education. Martin Luther King Jr. became the moral leader of the Civil Rights era, delivering his I Have a Dream speech during the nineteen sixty-three March on Washington.

The constitutional promise of equal protection came through the Fourteenth Amendment in eighteen sixty-eight, but was narrowly interpreted for nearly a century. Civil rights law finally realized that promise in the nineteen sixties. Yet economic disparities, mass incarceration, health inequities, and educational gaps persist as legacies of slavery and Jim Crow. This history reminds us that the struggle for equality in America is both foundational and ongoing.
